youtube_title: Illegal — But the Host Country Can't Prosecute? Diplomatic Immunity 🦝⚖️
caption: Under the Vienna Convention, accredited diplomats are immune from the host country's criminal courts — but their own country can waive it or prosecute them, and the host can require them to leave.
script: Some people in America can commit a felony right in front of a cop, and the country can't put them on trial. [disclaimer] It's called diplomatic immunity! It comes from a big international treaty, the Vienna Convention. And here's how the U.S. State Department explains it. Top diplomats have total immunity from the criminal courts of the country they're working in. So the law still applies to them. The country just can't put them on trial. Wild, right? But here's the twist. The diplomat can't give that immunity up. Only their home country can. And it has to say so clearly. So what happens if a diplomat does something really serious, like a violent crime, and their country won't give up the immunity? In America, the policy is, you have to leave. Get out! And the treaty says something else. Being immune here doesn't protect them back home. Their own country's courts can still go after them. Also, not everyone at an embassy gets the full deal. Consular officers usually only get immunity for their official work, and their staff get even less. And a fancy diplomatic passport alone isn't enough. In the State Department's own words, diplomatic immunity is not a license to flout the law. [loop] So before you assume a diplomat is above the law, remember
